arXiv:2605.02495v1 [cs.LG] 04 May 2026

Efficient Preference Poisoning Attack on Offline RLHF

Chenye Yang Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA Correspondence to: cyyyang@ucdavis.edu    Weiyu Xu Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA Correspondence to: weiyu-xu@uiowa.edu    Lifeng Lai Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of California, Davis, Davis, CA, USA Correspondence to: lflai@ucdavis.edu
Abstract

Offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipelines such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) train on a pre-collected preference dataset, which makes them vulnerable to preference poisoning attack. We study label flip attacks against log-linear DPO. We first illustrate that flipping one preference label induces a parameter-independent shift in the DPO gradient. Using this key property, we can then convert the targeted poisoning problem into a structured binary sparse approximation problem. To solve this problem, we develop two attack methods: Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A) and Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A). BAL-A embeds the binary flip selection problem into a binary-aware lattice and applies Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász reduction and Babai’s nearest plane algorithm; we provide sufficient conditions that enforce binary coefficients and recover the minimum-flip objective. BMP-A adapts binary matching pursuit to our non-normalized gradient dictionary and yields coherence-based recovery guarantees and robustness (impossibility) certificates for KK-flip budgets. Experiments on synthetic dictionaries and the Stanford Human Preferences dataset validate the theory and highlight how dictionary geometry governs attack success.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is a popular approach for aligning a learned policy with human preferences when an explicit reward function is hard to specify (Christiano et al., 2017; Casper et al., 2023). In many practical pipelines, the policy is trained from a pre-collected dataset of pairwise preference labels (Christiano et al., 2017; Bai et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023), which is referred to as offline RLHF (Xiong et al., 2023), to differentiate it from online RLHF where the policy is learned from real-time interactions with human feedbacks (Wang et al., 2023). Recent work has demonstrated that RLHF faces substantial security issues related to the reliability of the human preference data, i.e., when there are adversarial attacks on preferences or random noises in human preferences (Casper et al., 2023). The preference data can be manipulated by adversaries to mislead both offline and online RLHF to produce targeted outcomes (Wu et al., 2024a; Fu et al., 2025; Baumgärtner et al., 2024; Nika et al., 2025; Pathmanathan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025).

Two types of adversarial attack models are commonly studied in offline RLHF (Rando and Tramèr, 2023; Wu et al., 2024a; Baumgärtner et al., 2024; Nika et al., 2025): (i) label flip attack, which flips some labels within the original dataset; and (ii) data injection attack, which appends poisoned trajectories and preferences to the original dataset. In particular, (Rando and Tramèr, 2023; Wu et al., 2024a; Baumgärtner et al., 2024) provide valuable experimental results on the impact of label flip and data injection attacks, but focus less on the theoretical analysis. (Nika et al., 2025) provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the effectiveness of data injection attacks, showing that to mislead offline RLHF, the attacker needs to append numerous poisoned preference pairs, with size scaling linearly with the original dataset.

However, while label flip attacks on offline RLHF is practically plausible, a comprehensive theoretical study of such a setup remains an open problem. We aim to address this critical gap in this paper. Understanding this vulnerability is crucial for developing robust algorithms and ensuring the reliability of RLHF systems in real-world applications, e.g., designing helpful and harmless LLMs robust to adversarial attacks on training set. Compared with the data injection attack, the problem of understanding label flipping attack is more challenging: First, flips are limited to the original dataset: the attacker can only change labels on existing comparisons and cannot freely create arbitrary many new preference pairs. Second, the effect of flipping a single label on the learned policy is hard to predict, which makes it difficult to effectively choose which labels to attack.

To our best knowledge, this work is the first to provide a theoretical analysis of label flip attacks on offline RLHF, specifically on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) pipeline (Rafailov et al., 2023) under the log-linear policy class. Our focus on log-linear policies follows prior RLHF theory (Xiong et al., 2023; Chowdhury et al., 2024; Nika et al., 2025) and isolates the core geometric phenomenon that drives flip attacks. The main technical observation is simple but powerful: in log-linear DPO, flipping one preference label changes the gradient of the DPO objective by a vector that does not depend on the current policy parameter. The attacker’s problem can therefore be expressed in gradient space as selecting a subset of existing preference pairs whose flip-induced gradient shifts add up to (or closely approximate) a target vector, which is decided by the attacker’s desired policy to force the learner to adopt. We further show that controlling the gradient residual is a sufficient surrogate for policy-space attack success.

The reduction above implies that finding the optimal targeted flip attacks is a combinatorial problem and, in general, is computationally hard. To address this, we develop two algorithms with different focuses. First, for the general minimum-flip objective, we propose a Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A). BAL-A uses a lattice embedding that simultaneously penalizes residual error and non-binary coefficients, and then applies Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász (LLL) basis reduction and Babai’s nearest-plane algorithm to produce an integer solution that can be interpreted as a flip pattern. We further analyze how the embedding parameter controls the method and show that sufficiently large penalty enforces small integer coefficients and the proposed method finds the true minimum-flip solution under a separation condition. Second, when the attacker has a flip budget KK and the true attack is sparse, we propose Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A), a greedy method adapted from Binary Matching Pursuit (Wen and Li, 2021). BMP-A selects examples using normalized correlations to handle non-normalized gradient columns and admits coherence-based recovery guarantees. We also provide simple robustness certificates showing when no KK-flip attack can succeed.

We validate the theory on synthetic dictionaries and on dictionaries constructed from the Stanford Human Preferences (SHP) dataset (Ethayarajh et al., 2022). The synthetic setting allows controlled tests of the lattice penalty and the coherence conditions. On SHP, we observe that BAL-A’s success depends sharply on the penalty region predicted by the separation analysis, and that BMP-A benefits substantially from reducing dictionary coherence, supporting our theoretical results.

Additional Related Work: Adversarial attacks on bandit and standard RL problems have been extensively studied. In these setups, the attacker manipulates rewards, actions, and transitions to force the learner toward targeted behaviors. However, attacks on RLHF changes human feedback, such as preference labels, which are discrete, and indirectly shape the learned policy, making the effect of a single corruption harder to analyze. We summarize these additional related work in Appendix A.

2 Problem Formulation

2.1 Offline RLHF and DPO

In offline RLHF, we observe a fixed dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} consisting of pairwise preferences over two candidate actions/responses aa under the same state/prompt ss. We write each comparison as (s,a,a′,o)(s,a,a^{\prime},o), where o∈{+1,−1}o\in\{+1,-1\} encodes which action is preferred by the human labeler. o=+1o=+1 means a≻a′a\succ a^{\prime}, while o=−1o=-1 means a′≻aa^{\prime}\succ a. Given a reference policy μ\mu with parameter θμ\theta_{\mu}, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) trains a parametric policy πθ\pi_{\theta} directly from these comparisons, without explicitly fitting a reward model (Rafailov et al., 2023).

We focus on the log-linear policies for DPO, as defined in Definition 2.1. Log-linear policy class is commonly considered in RLHF literature (Xiong et al., 2023; Chowdhury et al., 2024; Nika et al., 2025), and it features many good properties in the further analysis.

Definition 2.1 (Log-linear Policy (Nika et al., 2025)).

Let ψ\psi be a dd-dimensional feature mapping ψ:𝒮×𝒜→ℝd\psi:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} with maxs,a⁡‖ψ⁡(s,a)‖≤1\max_{s,a}\|\psi(s,a)\|\leq 1. We consider the following class of log-linear policies ∀(s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜\forall(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A} where θ∈ℝd\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:

Πlog={πθ:πθ​(a∣s)=exp⁡(ψ​(s,a)⊤​θ)∑a′exp⁡(ψ​(s,a′)⊤​θ)}.\Pi^{\text{log}}=\left\{\pi_{\theta}:\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)=\frac{\exp\left(\psi(s,a)^{\top}\theta\right)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}}\exp\left(\psi(s,a^{\prime})^{\top}\theta\right)}\right\}.

Then, the DPO objective can be written as a regularized logistic loss over comparisons (Rafailov et al., 2023):

LDPO​(θ,𝒟)=−∑(s,a,a′,o)∈𝒟logσ(o⋅β(logπθ​(a|s)μ⁡(a|s)OPENOPEN−log⁡πθ​(a′|s)μ⁡(a′|s)))+λ2​∥θ−θμ∥22,\begin{split}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta;\mathcal{D})=&-\sum_{(s,a,a^{\prime},o)\in\mathcal{D}}\log\sigma\!\left(o\cdot\beta\left(\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a\,|\,s)}{\mu(a\,|\,s)}\right.\right.\\ &\left.\left.-\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{\prime}\,|\,s)}{\mu(a^{\prime}\,|\,s)}\right)\right)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\,\lVert\theta-\theta_{\mu}\rVert_{2}^{2},\end{split}

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function, β>0\beta>0 is a temperature parameter, and λ>0\lambda>0 is the regularization parameter. For reader’s convinience, we summarize the main steps of the derivation of DPO from the RLHF pipeline provided in (Rafailov et al., 2023) in Appendix B.

2.2 Preference Attack

We study label flip attacks on offline preference datasets. The attacker selects a subset of comparisons and flips their outcomes, equivalently changing oio_{i} to −oi-o_{i} on the chosen indices. The size of the dataset is fixed. Let x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} indicate which comparisons are flipped, and write 𝒟~​(x)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x) as the attacked dataset.

In this paper, a targeted label flip attacker’s optimization problem is formulated as:

minx∈{0,1}n⁡‖x‖0s.t.‖πθ^​(𝒟~​(x))−π†‖1≤ε,\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \|x\|_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bigl\|\pi_{\hat{\theta}(\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x))}-\pi^{\dagger}\bigr\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon,

Here θ^​(𝒟~​(x))\hat{\theta}(\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x)) is the DPO policy parameter trained on the attacked dataset, and πθ^​(𝒟~​(x))\pi_{\hat{\theta}(\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x))} is the correpsonding policy. In this formulation, the goal of the attacker is to force πθ^​(𝒟~​(x))\pi_{\hat{\theta}(\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x))} to align with a target policy π†\pi^{\dagger} (with parameter θ†\theta^{\dagger}) decided by the attacker, while modifying as few labels as possible.

We also consider a budgeted variant, in which the attacker can at most flip KK entries in the training dataset:

minx∈{0,1}n:‖x‖0≤K∥x∥0s.t.∥πθ^​(𝒟~​(x))−π†∥1≤ε,\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\ \|x\|_{0}\leq K}\ \|x\|_{0}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\bigl\|\pi_{\hat{\theta}(\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x))}-\pi^{\dagger}\bigr\|_{1}\leq\varepsilon,

3 Label Flip Attack on DPO

3.1 Effect of Label Flip Attack

The DPO optimization problem with log-linear policy can be written as minθ⁡LDPO​(θ,𝒟)\min_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta;\mathcal{D}). For sample ii: (si,ai,ai′,oi)(s_{i},a_{i},a_{i}^{\prime},o_{i}), the per-sample loss is

ℓi​(θ)=−log⁡σ⁡(oi​β​(log⁡πθ​(ai|si)μ⁡(ai|si)−log⁡πθ​(ai′|si)μ⁡(ai′|si))).\ell_{i}(\theta)=-\log\sigma\!\left(o_{i}\,\beta\left(\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{i}\,|\,s_{i})}{\mu(a_{i}\,|\,s_{i})}-\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{i}^{\prime}\,|\,s_{i})}{\mu(a_{i}^{\prime}\,|\,s_{i})}\right)\right). (1)

Using (1), the overall DPO loss can be written as:

LDPO​(θ,𝒟)=∑j∈𝒟ℓj​(θ)+λ2​∥θ−θμ∥2.L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta;\mathcal{D})=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{D}}\ell_{j}(\theta)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\theta-\theta_{\mu}\rVert^{2}.
Theorem 3.1 (Flip-induced gradient shift for log-linear DPO).

Fix a comparison (si,ai,ai′,oi)(s_{i},a_{i},a_{i}^{\prime},o_{i}) with oi∈{+1,−1}o_{i}\in\{+1,-1\}, and define the feature difference Δ​ψi:=ψ⁡(si,ai)−ψ⁡(si,ai′)∈ℝd\Delta\psi_{i}:=\psi(s_{i},a_{i})-\psi(s_{i},a_{i}^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let ℓi​(θ)\ell_{i}(\theta) be the per-sample DPO loss in (1), and let gi​(θ):=∇θℓi​(θ)g_{i}(\theta):=\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{i}(\theta). If we flip the label oio_{i} to o~i=−oi\tilde{o}_{i}=-o_{i}, and we have g~i​(θ)\tilde{g}_{i}(\theta) replacing the oio_{i} with o~i\tilde{o}_{i} in gi​(θ)g_{i}(\theta), then for every θ\theta the per-sample gradient changes by a constant vector that is independent of θ\theta:

Δ​gi:=g~i​(θ)−gi​(θ)=oi​β​Δ​ψi.\Delta g_{i}:=\tilde{g}_{i}(\theta)-g_{i}(\theta)\;=\;o_{i}\,\beta\,\Delta\psi_{i}.

Theorem 3.1 is the key structural property behind our attack formulation: each flipped comparison contributes a fixed “atom” in gradient space for all values of policy parameter θ\theta.

3.2 Formulate Label Flip Attack Problem

Using Theorem 3.1, when the attacker flip a set ℱ⊂𝒟\mathcal{F}\subset\mathcal{D}, the attacked gradient becomes:

∇θLDPO​(θ,𝒟~)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta;\tilde{\mathcal{D}}) =∑j∉ℱgj​(θ)+∑i∈ℱg~i​(θ)+λ⁡(θ−θμ)\displaystyle=\sum_{j\notin\mathcal{F}}g_{j}(\theta)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}\tilde{g}_{i}(\theta)+\lambda(\theta-\theta_{\mu})
=∇θLDPO​(θ,𝒟)+Δ​gℱ,\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta;\mathcal{D})+\Delta g_{\mathcal{F}},

where Δ​gℱ:=∑i∈ℱΔ​gi\Delta g_{\mathcal{F}}:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}\Delta g_{i} is a term depending on ℱ\mathcal{F}, but not on θ\theta. Strong convexity of LDPO​(θ,𝒟~)L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta;\tilde{\mathcal{D}}) (Lemma E.14 (Nika et al., 2025)) ensures that the first order condition (FOC) is enough to guarantee optimality. Then FOC minimizer for the attacked problem, θ~\tilde{\theta}, satisfies:

∇θLDPO​(θ~,𝒟~)=∇θLDPO​(θ~,𝒟)+Δ​gℱ=0.\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\tilde{\theta};\tilde{\mathcal{D}})=\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\tilde{\theta};\mathcal{D})+\Delta g_{\mathcal{F}}=0.

Now we need to study: if we want the learned policy θ~\tilde{\theta} to be some (target) policy θ†\theta^{\dagger}, what should the set ℱ\mathcal{F} be?

From the FOC above, we have:

g†:=∇θLDPO(θ†;𝒟)=−Δgℱ=−∑i∈ℱoiβΔψi,g^{\dagger}:=\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta^{\dagger};\mathcal{D})=-\Delta g_{\mathcal{F}}=-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}o_{i}\beta\,\Delta\psi_{i},

where we define g†g^{\dagger} as the gradient of the clean DPO loss at the target θ†\theta^{\dagger}.

For simplicity, denote vi=oi​β​Δ​ψiv_{i}=o_{i}\beta\Delta\psi_{i}, V=[v1,…,vn]∈ℝd×nV=[v_{1},\dots,v_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}. Then the label flip attack problem becomes:

minℱ|ℱ|s.t.∑i∈ℱvi=−g†.\min_{\mathcal{F}}\quad|\mathcal{F}|\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\sum_{i\in\mathcal{F}}v_{i}=-g^{\dagger}.

It can be seen as a binary sparse approximation problem:

minx∈{0,1}n𝟏⊤​xs.t.V​x=−g†.\displaystyle\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\quad\mathbf{1}^{\top}x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Vx=-g^{\dagger}.

We note that, in the label flip attack problem, the matrix VV is fixed and determined by the original dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and the target gradient −g†-g^{\dagger} is also fixed and determined by the target policy θ†\theta^{\dagger}. The vector xx is a binary vector indicating which samples to flip in the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

When we allow some approximation error ε\varepsilon in reaching the target policy θ†\theta^{\dagger}, we say that: a flip attack is exactly successful if V​x+g†=0Vx+g^{\dagger}=0, and approximately successful if ‖V​x+g†‖2≤ε.\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon. Thus, the exact and approximate flip attack problems can be written as:

minx∈{0,1}n𝟏⊤​xs.t.V​x+g†=0,\displaystyle\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\quad\mathbf{1}^{\top}x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Vx+g^{\dagger}=0, (2)

and

minx∈{0,1}n𝟏⊤​xs.t.‖V​x+g†‖2≤ε.\displaystyle\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\quad\mathbf{1}^{\top}x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon. (3)

3.3 From Gradient Residual to Policy Closeness

For log-linear policies, prior work justifies treating a parameter-space target as a surrogate for a policy-space success criterion. In particular, Lemma E.5 of (Nika et al., 2025) relate an ℓ1\ell_{1} policy-closeness constraint with tolerance ϵ\epsilon to a parameter-closeness constraint with tolerance ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime}: when ϵ′≤ϵ/(2​d)\epsilon^{\prime}\leq\epsilon/(2\sqrt{d}), parameter feasibility implies policy feasibility, and they also provide conditions for the reverse implication. Motivated by this equivalence, we analyze poisoning around a target parameter θ†\theta^{\dagger} and connect attack success to how flips perturb the DPO optimality conditions.

By construction,

∇θLDPO​(θ†,𝒟~)=∇θLDPO​(θ†,𝒟)+V​x=g†+V​x.\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta^{\dagger};\tilde{\mathcal{D}})=\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta^{\dagger};{\mathcal{D}})+Vx=g^{\dagger}+Vx. (4)

Hence, the approximate flip-attack constraint

‖V​x+g†‖2≤ε\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon (5)

is exactly a bound on the gradient residual at θ†\theta^{\dagger} for the poisoned objective, i.e., it enforces that θ†\theta^{\dagger} is an ε\varepsilon-stationary point of LDPO​(⋅,𝒟~)L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\;\cdot\;;\tilde{\mathcal{D}}). The following lemma shows that, under strong convexity, such approximate stationarity guarantees that training on 𝒟~\tilde{\mathcal{D}} produces a parameter (and thus a policy) close to the target.

Lemma 3.2 (Gradient residual to policy closeness).

Assume LDPO​(⋅,𝒟~)L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\;\cdot\;;\tilde{\mathcal{D}}) is differentiable and μ\mu-strongly convex in θ\theta, e.g., for log-linear DPO with ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization, see (Nika et al., 2025). Let θ^:=arg⁡minθ​LDPO​(θ,𝒟~)\hat{\theta}:=\arg\min_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta;\tilde{\mathcal{D}}) and define the trained policy πθ,𝒟~:=πθ^\pi_{\theta,\tilde{\mathcal{D}}}:=\pi_{\hat{\theta}}, with target policy π†:=πθ†\pi^{\dagger}:=\pi_{\theta^{\dagger}}. If ‖V​x+g†‖2≤ε\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon holds, equivalently ‖∇θLDPO​(θ†,𝒟~)‖2≤ε\|\nabla_{\theta}L_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\theta^{\dagger};\tilde{\mathcal{D}})\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon, then

‖θ^−θ†‖2≤ε/μ.\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon/\mu. (6)

Moreover, for log-linear policies this parameter bound implies the policy-space guarantee ‖πθ^−π†‖1≤ϵ\|\pi_{\hat{\theta}}-\pi^{\dagger}\|_{1}\leq\epsilon whenever ε≤μ​ϵ/(2​d)\varepsilon\leq\mu\,\epsilon/(2\sqrt{d}).

Lemma 3.2 justifies (5) as a sufficient condition for approximate attack success in policy space. This motivates our focus on the gradient perturbation at θ†\theta^{\dagger}; in the log-linear DPO case, the per-example flip induces a parameter-independent gradient shift, yielding a fixed dictionary of vectors (the columns of VV) and the binary selection formulation developed before.

3.4 Feasibility of Label Flip Attack

The feasibility question asks whether there exists x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} such that ‖V​x+g†‖2≤R\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq R, where R=0R=0 for (2) and R=εR=\varepsilon for (3). This decision problem is NP-hard in general. Equivalently, feasibility means that −g†-g^{\dagger} lies within distance RR of the finite attainable set 𝒜:={V​x:x∈{0,1}n}\mathcal{A}:=\{Vx:x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\}.

Therefore, we assume in the following that a feasible flip attack exists as in Assumption 3.3, and focus on finding the attack set ℱ\mathcal{F} and quantifying the cost of such an attack in terms of the number of flipped labels |ℱ||\mathcal{F}|.

Assumption 3.3 (Existence of feasible flip attack).

There exists a true binary attack vector x⋆∈{0,1}nx^{\star}\in\{0,1\}^{n} such that ‖V​x⋆+g†‖2≤R\|Vx^{\star}+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq R. In the exact problem we take R=0R=0, and in the approximate problem we take R=εR=\varepsilon.

3.5 Lower-bound of Flips

We now derive a simple lower bound on the number of flipped labels |ℱ||\mathcal{F}| required for a successful flipping attack.

Theorem 3.4 (Norm-based lower-bound of |ℱ||\mathcal{F}|).

If the attacker achieves the exact constraint in the exact problem (2), then the number of flips (|ℱ||\mathcal{F}| or 𝟏⊤​x\mathbf{1}^{\top}x) must satisfy |ℱ|≥‖g†‖2/(2​β)|\mathcal{F}|\geq\|g^{\dagger}\|_{2}/(2\beta). If the attacker is allowed tolerance ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0 and achieves the constraint in the approximate problem (3), then the number of flips must satisfy |ℱ|≥(‖g†‖2−ε)/(2​β)|\mathcal{F}|\geq(\|g^{\dagger}\|_{2}-\varepsilon)/(2\beta).

Theorem 3.4 shows that, the number of flips must grow at least linearly with the norm of the target gradient ‖g†‖2\|g^{\dagger}\|_{2}. The bounds do not require any structural assumptions on the attack matrix VV beyond the feature norm bound from Definition 2.1. They provide a simple necessary condition on |ℱ||\mathcal{F}| under the Assumption 3.3 of a feasible flip attack.

4 Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A)

In this section, we discuss why a standard lattice formulation for the closest vector problem (CVP) can not handle the flip attack problem, even they are similar. Motivated by the limitations, we introduce a binary-aware lattice embedding combined with Babai’s nearest-plane algorithm. We derive sufficient conditions under which the result is guaranteed to be binary and recover the minimum-flip.

4.1 Lattice Method and a Binary-aware Embedding

The exact flip attack is the minimum-flip feasibility problem:

minx∈{0,1}n⁡ 1⊤​xs.t.V​x+g†=0.\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Vx+g^{\dagger}=0. (7)

A common approximate relaxation approach replaces the hard constraint by residual minimization, which, however, results in a different objective:

minx∈{0,1}n⁡‖V​x+g†‖2.\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}. (8)

A natural relaxation of (8) is to allow integer coefficients,

minz∈ℤn⁡‖V​z+g†‖2,\min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\|Vz+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}, (9)

and view this as a CVP in the lattice (Lenstra et al., 1982) L:={V​z:z∈ℤn}⊂ℝdL:=\{Vz:z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with target t:=−g†t:=-g^{\dagger}. Indeed, dist⁡(L,t):=minz∈ℤn⁡‖V​z−t‖2=minz∈ℤn⁡‖V​z+g†‖2\mathrm{dist}(L,t):=\min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\|Vz-t\|_{2}=\min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\|Vz+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}. One can then apply lattice basis reduction (e.g., LLL (Lenstra et al., 1982)) and Babai’s nearest-plane algorithm (Babai, 1986) to obtain an integer vector z∈ℤnz\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} that approximately solves (9).

The lattice relaxation (9) is a natural starting point, but it does not directly match the binary minimum-flip model (7) in two key ways: binary coefficients, and minimum-flip objective. We summarize the mismatches in Appendix C.

These issues motivate a different design: rather than solving an unrestricted integer problem and truncating afterwards, we construct a binary-aware lattice embedding where non-binary coefficients are heavily penalized in the lattice norm, so that any sufficiently short lattice vector must already correspond to a (near) binary solution.

We work directly with the real-valued attack matrix VV and gradient g†g^{\dagger}. Assume that the flip-effect vectors are uniformly bounded ‖vi‖2≤B\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq B (B=2​βB=2\beta, shown in Appendix J.3), we build a lattice in ℝd+n\mathbb{R}^{d+n} using the (d+n)×(n+1)(d+n)\times(n+1) real basis

Bbin:=(V−g†M​In0),M>0,B_{\mathrm{bin}}:=\begin{pmatrix}V&-g^{\dagger}\\ MI_{n}&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad M>0,

whose columns are bi=(vi;M​ei)b_{i}=(v_{i};Me_{i}) for i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and bn+1=(−g†,0)b_{n+1}=(-g^{\dagger};0). For any integer vector z∈ℤnz\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, consider the coefficient vector u⁡(z):=(z,−1)∈ℤn+1u(z):=(z;-1)\in\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}, and the corresponding lattice vector

y⁡(z):=Bbin​u​(z)=(V​z+g†M​z)∈ℝd+n.y(z):=B_{\mathrm{bin}}u(z)=\begin{pmatrix}Vz+g^{\dagger}\\ Mz\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+n}.

Its squared norm decomposes as

‖y⁡(z)‖22=‖V​z+g†‖22+M2​‖z‖22.\|y(z)\|_{2}^{2}=\|Vz+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}+M^{2}\|z\|_{2}^{2}. (10)

Intuitively, the top block of BbinB_{\mathrm{bin}} measures how well zz approximates the target −g†-g^{\dagger} (attack effectiveness), while the bottom block penalizes the magnitude of the coefficients ziz_{i}. Thus, choosing MM sufficiently large discourages non-physical solutions with |zi|≥2|z_{i}|\geq 2, addressing the second mismatch above. Moreover, for binary flip indicators x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} we have ‖x‖22=𝟏⊤​x\|x\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbf{1}^{\top}x, so restricting (10) to binary vectors yields

minx∈{0,1}n⁡‖V​x+g†‖22+M2​ 1⊤​x,\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}+M^{2}\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}x, (11)

which couples residual minimization with the flip count and hence address the first mismatch. In particular, on the feasible set {x∈{0,1}n:V​x+g†=0}\{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:Vx+g^{\dagger}=0\} the residual term vanishes and (11) reduces to minimizing 𝟏⊤​x\mathbf{1}^{\top}x; therefore, whenever an exact attack is achievable, minimizing ‖y⁡(x)‖2\|y(x)\|_{2} over feasible binary solutions is equivalent to (2).

We summarize the practical attack method based on the binary-aware lattice embedding and Babai’s nearest-plane in Algorithm 1, shown in Appendix D. The inputs are the dataset matrix V∈ℝd×nV\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}, the target gradient g†∈ℝdg^{\dagger}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and a penalty parameter M>0M>0. The method first embeds the binary flip selection problem into a lattice by augmenting each column viv_{i} with a scaled identity component M​eiMe_{i}, so that nearest-lattice decoding corresponds to minimizing the binary-aware objective |V​z+g†|22+M2​|z|22|Vz+g^{\dagger}|_{2}^{2}+M^{2}|z|_{2}^{2} over integer vectors zz. It then applies LLL reduction to obtain a better-conditioned basis and uses Babai’s nearest-plane rounding to recover an integer coefficient vector, which is mapped back to the original coordinates and then truncated to produce a candidate flip pattern. For completeness, we provide the full step-by-step procedure (including the LLL and Babai) in Appendix D.

4.2 Theoretical Guarantees for BAL-A

4.2.1 Large MM enforces binary coefficients

We formalize how the penalty parameter MM controls the integer coefficients in the binary-aware embedding.

Lemma 4.1 (Coefficient bound for the shortest binary-aware lattice vector).

Assume the flip-effect vectors are bounded as ‖vi‖2≤B\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq B for all ii. Suppose there exists a binary flip attack x⋆∈{0,1}nx^{\star}\in\{0,1\}^{n} with support size K⋆:=‖x⋆‖0K^{\star}:=\|x^{\star}\|_{0} and residual ‖V​x⋆+g†‖2≤R\|Vx^{\star}+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq R. Let zopt∈arg⁡minz∈ℤn⁡‖y⁡(z)‖2z^{\mathrm{opt}}\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\|y(z)\|_{2} be any minimizer of the binary-aware lattice norm over ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Then there exists M0=M0​(B,R,K⋆)M_{0}=M_{0}(B,R,K^{\star}) such that for all M≥M0M\geq M_{0}, every coordinate satisfies |ziopt|≤1|z^{\mathrm{opt}}_{i}|\leq 1, i.e., zopt∈{−1,0,1}nz^{\mathrm{opt}}\in\{-1,0,1\}^{n}. One explicit sufficient choice is

M0=(B​K⋆+B2​K⋆+6​B​R+3​B2)/3.M_{0}=(B\sqrt{K^{\star}}+\sqrt{B^{2}K^{\star}+6BR+3B^{2}})/3. (12)

Lemma 4.1 shows that if there exists a reasonably good binary attack x⋆∈{0,1}nx^{\star}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, then for a sufficiently large MM the global minimizer of the embedded lattice norm over ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} cannot contain any coefficient with magnitude ≥2\geq 2.

Theorem 4.2 (Binary optimality under nonnegativity).

Under the assumptions of Lemma 4.1, assume additionally that we restrict to nonnegative coefficients, i.e., z∈ℤ≥0nz\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}, which is natural when each viv_{i} already encodes the flip direction. Let zopt∈arg⁡minz∈ℤ≥0n⁡‖y⁡(z)‖2z^{\mathrm{opt}}\in\arg\min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}}\|y(z)\|_{2}. If M≥M0​(B,R,K⋆)M\geq M_{0}(B,R,K^{\star}), then zopt∈{0,1}nz^{\mathrm{opt}}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and

‖y⁡(zopt)‖22=‖V​zopt+g†‖22+M2​‖zopt‖22≤‖y⁡(x⋆)‖22≤R2+M2​K⋆.\begin{split}\|y(z^{\mathrm{opt}})\|_{2}^{2}&=\|Vz^{\mathrm{opt}}+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}+M^{2}\|z^{\mathrm{opt}}\|_{2}^{2}\\ &\leq\|y(x^{\star})\|_{2}^{2}\leq R^{2}+M^{2}K^{\star}.\end{split}

Theorem 4.2 converts the coefficient bound from Lemma 4.1 into an actual {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} guarantee under the natural constraint z∈ℤ≥0nz\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}. Thus, the optimizer of the penalized embedding is a valid flip attack, which addresses the third mismatch.

4.2.2 Small MM recovers minimum-flip objective

We now analyze how MM controls the recovery of the minimum-flip objective in our flip attack problem.

Theorem 4.3 (Minimum-residual recovers minimum-flip).

Assume the exact flip attack is feasible, and let x⋆∈arg⁡minx∈{0,1}n​ 1⊤​x​ s.t. ​V​x+g†=0x^{\star}\in\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}x\text{ s.t. }Vx+g^{\dagger}=0. Define K⋆≔𝟏⊤​x⋆K^{\star}\coloneqq\mathbf{1}^{\top}x^{\star}. For each k∈{0,1,…,K⋆−1}k\in\{0,1,\dots,K^{\star}-1\} define the best kk-flip residual ρk:=minx∈{0,1}n: 1⊤​x=k∥Vx+g†∥2\rho_{k}:=\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}:\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}x=k}\ \|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}. Consider the binary-aware surrogate objective

FM​(x):=‖V​x+g†‖22+M2​ 1⊤​x,x∈{0,1}n.F_{M}(x):=\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}+M^{2}\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}x,\quad x\in\{0,1\}^{n}.

If MM satisfies the separation condition

ρk2>M2​(K⋆−k) for all ​k=0,1,…,K⋆−1,\rho_{k}^{2}\;>\;M^{2}\,(K^{\star}-k)\quad\text{ for all }k=0,1,\dots,K^{\star}-1, (13)

then every minimizer of minx∈{0,1}n⁡FM​(x)\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}F_{M}(x) is an optimal exact attack pattern; in particular, any minimizer is feasible (V​x+g†=0Vx+g^{\dagger}=0) and has 𝟏⊤​x=K⋆\mathbf{1}^{\top}x=K^{\star}.

Theorem 4.3 states that FM​(x)F_{M}(x) recovers the minimum-flip in exact attack case if all under-budget patterns (k<K⋆k<K^{\star}) satisfy separation condition, and any minimizer of FMF_{M} must be feasible and use exactly K⋆K^{\star} flips. This can be seen by a counterexample that when M≥‖g†‖2M\geq\|g^{\dagger}\|_{2}, the zero-flip solution x=0x=0 achieves the smallest objective value than any feasible solution with at least one flip.

The surrogate objective FMF_{M} trades off two goals: reducing the residual ‖V​x+g†‖2\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2} and promoting discrete binary coefficients. In general, these goals can conflict, so there is no single, universal choice of MM that guarantees recovering a feasible minimum-flip attack pattern for all instances. Moreover, if MM is chosen too large, the penalty can favor under-selection (too few flips) even when an exact solution exists. Formal counterexamples are given in Appendix E.

5 Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A)

In this section, we introduce the attack budget constraint KK and study the sparse KK-flip attack model. Then the KK-flip attack problem can be viewed as a sparse recovery problem with a binary constraint on the coefficients. We adapt the Binary Matching Pursuit (BMP) algorithm (Wen and Li, 2021) to our flip attack setting and further provide sufficient conditions under which no KK-flip attack can succeed.

5.1 Sparse KK-Flip Attack Model

Equivalent to the flip attack formulation in Section 3.4, we define the minimum number of flips required for approximate success as

K⋆:=minx∈{0,1}n𝟏⊤​xs.t.‖V​x+g†‖2≤R,K^{\star}:=\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\quad\mathbf{1}^{\top}x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq R, (14)

and ask whether K⋆<∞K^{\star}<\infty (i.e., whether the constraint set is nonempty). Problem (14) is a binary optimization problem and is NP-hard in general.

As in classical sparse recovery, our analysis assumes that there exists an underlying feasible sparse solution to the attack constraint.

Assumption 5.1 (Existence of a feasible K⋆K^{\star}-flip attack).

There exists a true binary attack vector x⋆∈{0,1}nx^{\star}\in\{0,1\}^{n} and an integer K⋆≥1K^{\star}\geq 1 such that ‖x⋆‖0=K⋆\|x^{\star}\|_{0}=K^{\star} and ‖V​x⋆+g†‖2≤R\|Vx^{\star}+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq R. In the exact problem we take R=0R=0, and in the approximate problem we take R=εR=\varepsilon.

In practice, an adversary is typically constrained to modify only a small fraction of the data. We therefore focus on the sparse attack regime, where K⋆K^{\star} is small. This motivates a budgeted KK-flip model: for a given budget K≥K⋆K\geq K^{\star}, we restrict attention to attacks with ‖x‖0≤K\|x\|_{0}\leq K and study (i) impossibility conditions under which no such sparse attack can succeed, and (ii) algorithmic recovery of a successful sparse attack when it exists. Formally, we assume

Assumption 5.2 (Sparse attack model).

‖x⋆‖0≤K\|x^{\star}\|_{0}\leq K (equivalently, K⋆≤KK^{\star}\leq K).

In this way, KK simultaneously models the attacker’s budget and provides a robustness scale: larger KK makes attacks easier, while small KK may render attacks impossible.

5.2 BMP-A’s Connection to Sparse Recovery

Our sparse flip-attack formulation is closely related to classical sparse recovery / sparse approximation. In the standard sparse recovery model, one observes (Tropp and Gilbert, 2007; Wen and Li, 2021) y=A​x⋆+ey=Ax^{\star}+e, where A∈ℝd×nA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} is a dictionary (or sensing matrix), x⋆∈ℝnx^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is KK-sparse, and ee models noise. The goal is to identify the sparse support (and possibly the coefficients) of x⋆x^{\star} from yy. A canonical greedy method is Orthogonal Matching Pursuit (OMP) (Tropp and Gilbert, 2007), which iteratively selects the column of AA most correlated with the current residual and then updates the residual after incorporating the selected atom.

In our setting, the “measurement” vector is the attack target y:=−g†y:=-g^{\dagger}, the dictionary is the per-sample gradient contribution matrix A:=VA:=V, and the attack is to find a sparse binary selector x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} such that V​x≈−g†Vx\approx-g^{\dagger}, i.e., yy is approximated by a sum of a small number of columns of VV. Compared with classical sparse recovery, our coefficients are constrained to be binary (fixed to +1+1 on the chosen support), so the main task is support selection rather than continuous coefficient estimation. This viewpoint motivates pursuit-style greedy solvers, leading to our Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A) in Algorithm 2, shown in Appendix G.

In BMP-A, we adapt BMP (Wen and Li, 2021) to our setting while keeping the algorithm expressed in terms of the original non-normalized columns viv_{i} of VV and a binary selection vector x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n}. Starting from r0=yr^{0}=y and x0=0x^{0}=0, BMP-A greedily picks one unselected index using the normalized score |⟨vi,r⟩|/‖vi‖2|\langle v_{i},r\rangle|/\|v_{i}\|_{2} per iteration and updates the residual by subtracting the selected original column r←r−vitr\leftarrow r-v_{i_{t}}. It stops after KK iterations when the budget is exhausted, or when the residual is small ‖r‖2≤ε\|r\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon.

Most sparse-recovery analyses, including those for BMP (Wen and Li, 2021), assume that the dictionary columns are normalized to unit ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm. In our problem, the columns viv_{i} of VV need not satisfy ‖vi‖2=1\|v_{i}\|_{2}=1, so BMP-A selects indices using normalized correlations. Define

ai\displaystyle a_{i} :=‖vi‖2>0,\displaystyle:=\|v_{i}\|_{2}>0, ui\displaystyle u_{i} :=viai,\displaystyle:=\frac{v_{i}}{a_{i}},
D\displaystyle D :=diag⁡(a1,…,an),\displaystyle:=\mathrm{diag}(a_{1},\dots,a_{n}), U\displaystyle U :=[u1,…,un]=V​D−1.\displaystyle:=[u_{1},\dots,u_{n}]=VD^{-1}.

Then for any binary attack x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n}, we haveV​x=U​zVx=Uz with z:=D​xz:=Dx, so zz is KK-sparse and has the same support as xx, but with nonzero amplitudes {ai:xi=1}\{a_{i}:x_{i}=1\} rather than 11. This normalization explains the BMP-A selection rule: at each step, it∈arg⁡maxi∈[n]∖Γ⁡|⟨vi,r⟩|‖vi‖2=arg⁡maxi∈[n]∖Γ​|⟨ui,r⟩|i_{t}\in\arg\max_{i\in[n]\setminus\Gamma}\ \frac{|\langle v_{i},r\rangle|}{\|v_{i}\|_{2}}=\arg\max_{i\in[n]\setminus\Gamma}\ |\langle u_{i},r\rangle|, which is the standard correlation criterion under the unit-norm dictionary UU. Likewise, mutual coherence is naturally defined using normalized directions,

μ⁡(V):=maxi≠j⁡|⟨vi,vj⟩|‖vi‖2​‖vj‖2=maxi≠j⁡|⟨ui,uj⟩|.\mu(V):=\max_{i\neq j}\frac{|\langle v_{i},v_{j}\rangle|}{\|v_{i}\|_{2}\|v_{j}\|_{2}}=\max_{i\neq j}|\langle u_{i},u_{j}\rangle|.

Note, however, that passing from (V,x)(V,x) to (U,z)(U,z) changes the nonzero magnitudes from 11 to aia_{i}; consequently, recovery guarantees stated for unit-norm dictionaries with equal-magnitude nonzeros require a mild adjustment that depends on the column-norm ratio.

5.3 Theoretical Guarantees for BMP-A

5.3.1 Recovery of x⋆x^{\star} within budget KK

Under standard binary sparse-recovery conditions, we specially adapt the following guarantees to our setting.

Theorem 5.3 (Recovery under coherence).

Under the K⋆K^{\star}-flip Assumption 5.1. Let μ⁡(V)\mu(V) be defined as above and b:=min1≤i≤n⁡‖vi‖2b:=\min_{1\leq i\leq n}\|v_{i}\|_{2}, B:=max1≤i≤n⁡‖vi‖2B:=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|v_{i}\|_{2}. If

μ⁡(V)<b(2​K⋆−1)​B\mu(V)<\frac{b}{(2K^{\star}-1)B} (15)

and

ε<(b−(2​K⋆−1)​μ​(V)​B)/2,\varepsilon<(b-(2K^{\star}-1)\mu(V)B)/2, (16)

then BMP-A (Algorithm 2), selects an index in supp⁡(x⋆)\mathrm{supp}(x^{\star}) at each iteration. Consequently, after K⋆K^{\star} iterations it exactly recovers supp⁡(x⋆)\mathrm{supp}(x^{\star}) and returns a binary vector x^\hat{x} with supp⁡(x^)=supp⁡(x⋆)\mathrm{supp}(\hat{x})=\mathrm{supp}(x^{\star}). Moreover, once the correct support has been selected, rK⋆=y−V​x^=y−V​x⋆=er^{K^{\star}}=y-V\hat{x}=y-Vx^{\star}=e, so the stopping rule ‖r‖2≤ε\|r\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon triggers no later than iteration K⋆K^{\star}.

Theorem 5.3 is the direct analog of the coherence condition in (Wen and Li, 2021), but adapted to non-normalized columns through the norm range b≤‖vi‖2≤Bb\leq\|v_{i}\|_{2}\leq B. Let ρ:=B/b\rho:=B/b, the mutual coherence requirement scales as μ⁡(V)≲1(2​K⋆−1)​ρ\mu(V)\lesssim\frac{1}{(2K^{\star}-1)\rho}: highly non-uniform column norms (large ρ\rho) make recovery more stringent. When b=Bb=B, e.g., after normalization, (15)–(16) reduce to the standard guarantee of (Wen and Li, 2021).

5.3.2 Impossibility conditions for KK-flip attack

We now give sufficient conditions under which no KK-flip attack can succeed, independent of specific attack algorithms.

Theorem 5.4 (Spectral norm and coherence impossibility).

Let B:=maxi⁡‖vi‖2B:=\max_{i}\|v_{i}\|_{2}, μ⁡(V)\mu(V) be defined as above, and ‖V‖2\|V\|_{2} be the spectral norm of VV. Fix a budget K≥1K\geq 1 and tolerance ε≥0\varepsilon\geq 0. If

‖g†‖2−ε>K​‖V‖2,\|g^{\dagger}\|_{2}-\varepsilon>\sqrt{K}\|V\|_{2}, (17)

or

(‖g†‖2−ε)2>B2​(K+μ⁡(V)​K​(K−1)),\bigl(\|g^{\dagger}\|_{2}-\varepsilon\bigr)^{2}>B^{2}\bigl(K+\mu(V)\,K(K-1)\bigr), (18)

then there does not exist any x∈{0,1}nx\in\{0,1\}^{n} with ‖x‖0≤K\|x\|_{0}\leq K such that ‖V​x+g†‖2≤ε\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq\varepsilon. In particular, (17) is a spectral-norm certificate, while (18) is a coherence-based refinement.

Theorem 5.4 provides sufficient conditions under which a KK-flip attacker cannot drive the gradient residual at θ†\theta^{\dagger} below ε\varepsilon. It shows that the success of any label flip attack is limited by the geometry and scale of the flip-effect dictionary VV. The spectral-norm condition (17) is universal: it only depends on the global operator norm ‖V‖2\|V\|_{2} and scales as K\sqrt{K}. The coherence condition (18) is more refined: it separates the per-example strength BB from the directional similarity μ⁡(V)\mu(V). When columns are weak (small BB) and point in diverse directions (small μ⁡(V)\mu(V)), even the best choice of KK flips cannot create a large enough shift to cancel g†g^{\dagger}. These are certificates of robustness of DPO: failing them does not imply an attack exists, but satisfying them rules out all KK-flip attacks, independent of specific attack algorithms.

6 Experiments and Results

In this section, we evaluate the proposed methods on both synthetic and real preference datasets.

6.1 Setup

We construct experiments with a K⋆K^{\star}-flip ground truth, following Assumption 3.3. We sample x⋆∈{0,1}nx^{\star}\in\{0,1\}^{n} with ‖x⋆‖0=K⋆\|x^{\star}\|_{0}=K^{\star} and set the target vector as t:=V​x⋆=−g†t:=Vx^{\star}=-g^{\dagger}, so the exact constraint is feasible by design. Given an output x^\hat{x}, we report support recovery against x⋆x^{\star}, e.g., true positive rate (TPR), and the residual ‖V​x^−t‖2\|V\hat{x}-t\|_{2}.

For synthetic data, we construct synthetic VV from normalized random Gaussian columns. To validate the BAL-A separation behavior, we use a dictionary with V∈ℝ64×20V\in\mathbb{R}^{64\times 20} and K⋆=5K^{\star}=5 and sweep the lattice penalty MM over 2525 log-spaced values; we apply LLL pre-reduction (δ=0.75\delta=0.75) before Babai and run 200200 Monte Carlo trials. To validate BMP-A in the sparse regime, we fix a single low-coherence dictionary V∈ℝ200×200V\in\mathbb{R}^{200\times 200} and sweep the true sparsity level K⋆K^{\star}; for each K⋆K^{\star} we run 200200 trials and run BMP-A for exactly K⋆K^{\star} iterations.

For real data, we construct VV from the Stanford Human Preferences (SHP) dataset (Ethayarajh et al., 2022) by training a log-linear DPO model and forming the per-example flip-induced gradient shifts. For BAL-A, we use a smaller attacked subset (n=50n=50, K⋆=7K^{\star}=7) and sweep MM. For BMP-A, we use a larger subset (n=401n=401, K⋆=10K^{\star}=10) and run BMP-A up to budget K=15K=15 with tolerance ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}, comparing a random subset to a low-coherence subset of the same size. On SHP we use the same main metrics as in the synthetic experiments (support recovery and residual reduction), and we additionally report coherence statistics to highlight differences in dictionary geometry. We also compare the DPO model trained on attacked subset of SHP 𝒟~​(x^)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(\hat{x}) to that trained on 𝒟~​(x⋆)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x^{\star}). Full setup details are deferred to Appendix H, and the SHP plots are deferred to Appendix I.

6.2 Results

6.2.1 Validate BAL-A theory on synthetic VV

Figure 1 shows the support TPR of BAL-A as the lattice penalty MM varies on a Gaussian synthetic dictionary. BAL-A recovers the true support almost perfectly for small MM, but the recall drops quickly once MM becomes moderately large. The transition happens around the separation threshold Mall sep≈0.68M_{\text{all sep}}\approx 0.68 (vertical line) satisfying all of those in Theorem 4.3: below this value all the separation conditions hold and recovery is stable, while above it BAL-A increasingly miss the true flips. The binary-coefficient sufficient bound M0≈1.69M_{0}\approx 1.69 is overly conservative in this setting.

6.2.2 Validate BMP-A theory on synthetic VV

Figure 2 evaluates BMP-A on a fixed low-coherence synthetic dictionary while increasing the true number of flips K⋆K^{\star}. The constructed matrix has empirical coherence μ⁡(V)≈0.197\mu(V)\approx 0.197 and the corresponding guarantee in Theorem 5.3 only covers up to Kcoh=3K_{\text{coh}}=3 (vertical line). Within this guaranteed region, BMP-A achieves perfect support recovery. Beyond KcohK_{\text{coh}}, the sufficient condition no longer applies, yet BMP-A still maintains high TPR and degrades gradually as K⋆K^{\star} grows, indicating that the coherence bound is conservative in this synthetic setting and that BMP-A remains effective outside the sufficient guarantee.

6.2.3 Results on real data set SHP

We also evaluate BAL-A and BMP-A on dictionaries constructed from the SHP dataset. Compared to the synthetic setting, SHP dictionaries are higher-dimensional (e.g., d=768d=768) and exhibit different geometry, including stronger correlations and non-uniform column norms. We report the same main metrics as in the synthetic experiments (support recovery and residual reduction), and for BMP-A we additionally compare a random subset to a low-coherence subset of the same size to isolate the role of dictionary coherence. We also report downstream diagnostics that compare the DPO model trained on the recovered flip set x^\hat{x} to that trained on the ground-truth flip set x⋆x^{\star}. The SHP plots and detailed discussion are deferred to Appendix I.

7 Conclusion

We have studied label flip preference attacks on offline RLHF, specifically targeting the log-linear DPO pipeline. We have illustrated the effect of flipping one preference label on the gradient of the DPO objective, and converted the attack problem to a binary sparse approximation problem in the per-sample gradient space. To solve it, we have proposed BAL-A algorithm, and provided sufficient conditions for binary coefficients and objective recovering. In practice, with budget KK, we have also considered the KK-flip attack problem and propose BMP-A, and provided a coherence-based recovery guarantee. We have also provided two impossibility conditions under which no KK-flip attack can succeed. We have provided extensive experiments on both synthetic and real data to validate the theory.

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Appendix A Introduction: Additional Related Work

A.1 Adversarial Attacks on Bandits

A line of work has studied adversarial attacks on bandit problems, including multi-armed bandits (MAB) (Jun et al., 2018; Liu and Shroff, 2019; Liu and Lai, 2020; Ma and Zhou, 2023; Yang et al., 2024), linear contextual bandits (Ma et al., 2018; Garcelon et al., 2020; Liu and Lai, 2021a), and dueling bandits (Gajane et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2021; Saha et al., 2021). These works have demonstrated that bandit algorithms are vulnerable to adversarial manipulation.

In the MAB setting, the learner takes an action by selecting one arm each round and observes its reward (Robbins, 1952; Auer et al., 1995; Auer et al., 2002). An adversary can manipulate the reward signals to mislead the learning algorithm into selecting a target arm more frequently (Jun et al., 2018; Ma and Zhou, 2023; Liu and Shroff, 2019), or corrupt the action signals to influence the learning process (Liu and Lai, 2020). Most of these existing work focused on the stationary random rewards setting, in which the distribution of reward of each arm does not change over time. Some (Ma and Zhou, 2023) studied the adversarial setting, in which the reward given by the environment can be arbitrarily chosen (Auer et al., 2002; Zimmert and Seldin, 2019). Other work (Yang et al., 2024) considered non-stationary stochastic bandits, in which the reward distribution of each arm can change over time but with some constraints on the total amount of changes (Garivier and Moulines, 2011; Besbes et al., 2014; Auer et al., 2019; Besbes et al., 2019; Cheung et al., 2022).

In linear contextual bandits, the expected reward is modeled as a linear function of the context features (Auer, 2002; Abe et al., 2003; Li et al., 2010). Existing works on adversarial attacks against linear contextual bandits focus on the reward poisoning (Ma et al., 2018; Garcelon et al., 2020), where the attacker manipulates the reward signal; context poisoning (Garcelon et al., 2020), where the adversary modifies the context observed without changing the reward associated with the context; and action poisoning (Liu and Lai, 2021a), where the adversary changes the action selected by the learner.

In dueling bandits, the learner selects a pair of arms each round and observes relative feedback indicating which arm is preferred (Yue et al., 2012; Zoghi et al., 2014; Sui et al., 2018). Prior work studies stochastic dueling bandits with adversarial corruption, where an attacker can corrupt pairwise outcomes (Agarwal et al., 2021). Other works consider fully adversarial preference models, which can be viewed as an extreme form of corruption (Gajane et al., 2015; Saha et al., 2021).

A.2 Adversarial Attacks on Standard Reinforcement Learning

Adversarial attacks on standard reinforcement learning (RL) have been widely studied under different poisoning models, where the attacker modifies the learning signals to mislead the learned policy. Common corruptions include reward poisoning (manipulating reward or cost signals) (Huang and Zhu, 2019; Zhang et al., 2020; Rakhsha et al., 2020; Rakhsha et al., 2021; Banihashem et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025), action poisoning (manipulating the agent’s action before it is applied) (Liu and Lai, 2021b), and more general environment poisoning such as manipulating transition dynamics (Rakhsha et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2021). Poisoning has also been studied in batch setting (Ma et al., 2019), and in dynamics-agnostic settings where attacker must learn to attack from interaction (Sun et al., 2020b; Liu and Lai, 2021b; Rakhsha et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2022; Li et al., 2025).

Beyond single-agent RL, adversarial attacks have been considered in more complex settings, including multi-agent RL where the attacker can corrupt rewards and/or actions (Liu and Lai, 2023; Wu et al., 2023), and federated RL where poisoning can exploit both the RL dynamics and the federated aggregation mechanism (Ma et al., 2024). There is also work that characterizes limits of reward-only or action-only poisoning in episodic RL (Rangi et al., 2022), as well as work that studies optimal attack in attacker’s Markov decision process (McMahan et al., 2024). In addition, many attacks are studied specifically in deep RL, where policies are neural networks and the attacker perturbs high-dimensional observations to induce harmful actions at decision time (Huang et al., 2017; Kos and Song, 2017; Lin et al., 2017; Pattanaik et al., 2017; Mandlekar et al., 2017; Pan et al., 2019; Gleave et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2020a),

A.3 Adversarial Attacks on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

RLHF relies on human preference data as the training source, which is inherently different from bandit or standard RL settings that use numerical rewards. Recent works have shown that RLHF faces substantial security issues related to the reliability of preference data, i.e., when there are adversarial attacks on preferences or random noises in human preferences (Casper et al., 2023). In offline RLHF (Xiong et al., 2023), where the learner trains on a pre-collected preference dataset (Christiano et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2023; Rafailov et al., 2023), preference data can be manipulated by adversaries to mislead training and induce targeted behaviors (Wu et al., 2024a; Rando and Tramèr, 2023; Baumgärtner et al., 2024; Pathmanathan et al., 2024; Nika et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025; Pathmanathan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). Most existing studies demonstrate this vulnerability from data injection attacks and label flip attacks experimentally on large-scale models (Rando and Tramèr, 2023; Wu et al., 2024a; Baumgärtner et al., 2024; Pathmanathan et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2025; Pathmanathan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), while (Nika et al., 2025) provides a comprehensive theoretical analysis of data injection attacks and shows that a large appended poisoned preference set may be needed to mislead offline RLHF. In online RLHF, where the agent learns from real-time interactions with human feedbacks (Chen et al., 2022; Saha et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2023; Wu and Sun, 2024) adversaries also attack the preference to manipulate the learning process (Yang et al., 2025).

Besides adversarial poisoning, the preference data is also inherently noisy due to annotation difficulty, limited expert availability, and systematic differences across annotators (Casper et al., 2023; Yan et al., 2024). Such noise can lead to hard-to-predict behaviors and potential biases in aligned model outputs. Accordingly, a line of work studies robustness of offline RLHF under noisy or partially corrupted preferences (Yan et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024; Mandal et al., 2024; Chowdhury et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024b). These works typically focus on random corruption models or random noise rather than a targeted adversarial attacker that strategically selects which comparisons to corrupt.

Compared with attacks on standard RL and bandits, attacks on RLHF face an additional challenge: the feedback is discrete preference data, and its effect on the learned policy is less direct and harder to predict. Moreover, in label flip attack problem for offline RLHF, the attacker is restricted to manipulating a fixed preference dataset, rather than freely manipulating rewards or transitions or generating new comparison pairs. Our work focuses on this practically plausible label flip threat model and provides a theoretical analysis for DPO under the log-linear policy class.

Appendix B Problem Formulation: Offline RLHF Pipeline and DPO Derivation (Rafailov et al., 2023)

This appendix provides a short summary that connects the standard offline RLHF pipeline to the DPO objective used in the main paper. We note that these derivations were done in (Rafailov et al., 2023) with a slightly different notation. We include them here for readers’ convenience. The subsequent attack formulation and guarantees do not depend on the intermediate reward-modeling step.

RLHF frameworks usually combine three interconnected processes: feedback collection, reward modeling, and policy optimization (Christiano et al., 2017; Casper et al., 2023). Once given two answers a1a_{1} and a2a_{2} for the same prompt ss, the human labeler is asked to compare the two answers and give their preference, denoted as aw≻al|sa_{w}\succ a_{l}\mid s where awa_{w} is the preferred answer and ala_{l} is the dispreferred answer in the pair (a1,a2)(a_{1},a_{2}). Note that to match the notation in (Rafailov et al., 2023), this appendix writes each comparison as (s,aw,al)(s,a_{w},a_{l}), so the label is implicit. This is equivalent to the main-text notation (s,a,a′,o)(s,a,a^{\prime},o) with o∈{+1,−1}o\in\{+1,-1\} by setting

(aw,al)={(a,a′),o=+1,(a′,a),o=−1.(a_{w},a_{l})=\begin{cases}(a,a^{\prime}),&o=+1,\\ (a^{\prime},a),&o=-1.\end{cases}

Equivalently, given (s,aw,al)(s,a_{w},a_{l}) one can take (s,a,a′,o)=(s,aw,al,+1)(s,a,a^{\prime},o)=(s,a_{w},a_{l},+1).

We assume that there is some latent reward model r∗​(a,s)r^{*}(a,s) for the prompt ss and the answer aa, which can not be observed by anyone. Bradley-Terry model (Bradley and Terry, 1952) describes the human preference distribution p∗p^{*} for pairwise comparisons:

p∗​(a1≻a2∣s)=exp⁡(r∗​(s,a1))exp⁡(r∗​(s,a1))+exp⁡(r∗​(s,a2)).p^{*}(a_{1}\succ a_{2}\mid s)=\frac{\exp(r^{*}(s,a_{1}))}{\exp(r^{*}(s,a_{1}))+\exp(r^{*}(s,a_{2}))}.

In the offline RLHF setting, the agent has access to a static dataset of comparisons 𝒟={s(i),aw(i),al(i)}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{s^{(i)},a_{w}^{(i)},a_{l}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} sampled from p∗p^{*}. Using the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the agent can learn a reward model rϕ​(s,a)r_{\phi}(s,a) parameterized by ϕ\phi via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). The negative log-likelihood loss function is defined as:

LRLHF​(rϕ,𝒟)=−𝔼(s,aw,al)∼𝒟​[log⁡σ⁡(rϕ​(s,aw)−rϕ​(s,al))],L_{\text{RLHF}}(r_{\phi},\mathcal{D})=-\mathbb{E}_{(s,a_{w},a_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma(r_{\phi}(s,a_{w})-r_{\phi}(s,a_{l}))\right],

where σ⁡(x)=11+exp⁡(−x)\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-x)} is the sigmoid function for the Bradley-Terry model. Then a RL algorithm is used to optimize a policy πθ\pi_{\theta} parameterized by θ\theta with the learned reward model rϕ​(s,a)r_{\phi}(s,a):

maxπθ𝔼s∼𝒟,a∼πθ​(a∣s)[rϕ(s,a)−β𝔻KL[πθ(a∣s)∥πref(a∣s)]],\begin{split}\max_{\pi_{\theta}}&\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D},\,a\sim\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)}\left[r_{\phi}(s,a)-\beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\left[\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid s)\right]\right],\end{split}

where β\beta is a parameter controlling the trade-off between learning the human preferences and following the reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}.

To avoid the computational cost of policy optimization by reinforcement learning in large-scale problems, DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) is proposed to directly optimize the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} with the preference data (s,aw,al)(s,a_{w},a_{l}). Solving the policy optimization problem leads to the following optimal solution:

πr​(a∣s)=1Z⁡(s)​πref​(a∣s)​exp⁡(1β​r​(s,a)),\pi_{r}(a\mid s)=\frac{1}{Z(s)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(a\mid s)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(s,a)\right),

where Z⁡(s)=∑aπref​(a∣s)​exp⁡(1β​r​(s,a))Z(s)=\sum_{a}\pi_{\text{ref}}(a\mid s)\exp\left(\frac{1}{\beta}r(s,a)\right) is the partition function. Rearranging the above equation leads to:

r⁡(s,a)=β​log⁡πr​(a∣s)πref​(a∣s)+β​log⁡Z⁡(s).r(s,a)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_{r}(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a\mid s)}+\beta\log Z(s).

Applying this reparameterization to the ground-truth reward function r∗r^{*} and corresponding optimal policy π∗\pi^{*}, and the Bradley-Terry model, we have:

p∗​(a1≻a2∣s)=11+exp⁡(β​log⁡π∗​(a2∣s)πref​(a2∣s)−β​log⁡π∗​(a1∣s)πref​(a1∣s)).p^{*}(a_{1}\succ a_{2}\mid s)=\frac{1}{1+\exp\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi^{*}(a_{2}\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a_{2}\mid s)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi^{*}(a_{1}\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a_{1}\mid s)}\right)}.

In this way, we model the human preference probability as a function of the optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} rather than the reward function r∗r^{*}. Therefore, the loss function in MLE for parameterized policy πθ\pi_{\theta} can be rewritten as:

LDPO​(πθ,πref)=−𝔼(s,aw,al)∼𝒟​[log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(aw∣s)πref​(aw∣s)−β​log⁡πθ​(al∣s)πref​(al∣s))].\begin{split}L_{\text{DPO}}(\pi_{\theta};\pi_{\text{ref}})=&-\mathbb{E}_{(s,a_{w},a_{l})\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{w}\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a_{w}\mid s)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{l}\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a_{l}\mid s)}\right)\right].\end{split}

Solving this estimation problem leads to the desired policy πθ\pi_{\theta}.

Appendix C BAL-A: Key Mismatches of the Standard Lattice Relaxation

This standard lattice approach has three key mismatches with our flip model:

  1. 1.

    Objective mismatch (minimum residual vs. minimum flips). The CVP-style formulation focuses on minimizing the residual minx∈{0,1}n⁡‖V​x+g†‖2\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}, whereas our flip attack is a minimum-cardinality problem: minx∈{0,1}n⁡ 1⊤​x\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}x. Even when an exact attack is feasible (so the residual is zero), residual minimization alone does not distinguish among multiple feasible solutions and therefore does not, in general, recover the minimum-flip pattern.

  2. 2.

    Unbounded integer coefficients. In (9), the coefficients ziz_{i} can be arbitrary integers, corresponding to “using” the same flip-effect viv_{i} multiple times. In our setting, each data point can be flipped at most once, so the admissible coefficients must lie in {0,1}\{0,1\}. Large integer coefficients are not meaningful as physical flip patterns.

  3. 3.

    No guaranteed truncation. A common workaround is to truncate an integer solution to the binary hypercube, e.g., xi=𝟏{zi≥1}x_{i}=\mathbf{1}\{z_{i}\geq 1\}. This nonlinear projection can destroy the relationship between ‖V​z+g†‖2\|Vz+g^{\dagger}\|_{2} and ‖V​x+g†‖2\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}, and there is no guarantee that a near-optimal integer solution leads to a near-optimal binary solution.

Appendix D BAL-A: Full Binary-Aware Lattice Attack Algorithm

The Binary-Aware Lattice Attack (BAL-A) algorithm is summarized in Algorithm 1.

Here we provide more details on each step of BAL-A:

  1. 1.

    Construct the binary-aware lattice basis and target.

    1. (a)

      Form the extended basis

      Be=[b1,…,bn]∈ℝ(d+n)×n,bi:=(viM​ei),B_{e}=[b_{1},\dots,b_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+n)\times n},\quad b_{i}:=\begin{pmatrix}v_{i}\\ Me_{i}\end{pmatrix},

      where i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,n and eie_{i} is the ii-th standard basis vector in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

    2. (b)

      Define the target vector

      t:=(−g†0)∈ℝd+n.t:=\begin{pmatrix}-g^{\dagger}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+n}.

      Minimizing ‖Be​x−t‖2\|B_{e}x-t\|_{2} over x∈ℤnx\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} is equivalent to minimizing ‖V​x+g†‖22+M2​‖x‖22\|Vx+g^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}+M^{2}\|x\|_{2}^{2} in the binary-aware objective.

  2. 2.

    Apply LLL basis reduction (Lenstra et al., 1982) to basis BeB_{e}.

    1. (a)

      Fix a parameter δ∈(1/4,1)\delta\in(1/4,1), e.g. δ=3/4\delta=3/4.

    2. (b)

      Initialize the basis vectors b1,…,bnb_{1},\dots,b_{n} as the columns of BeB_{e} and compute their Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization:

      bi∗,μi,j,1≤j<i≤n,b_{i}^{\ast},\ \mu_{i,j},\quad 1\leq j<i\leq n,

      where

      bi∗=bi−∑j<iμi,j​bj∗,μi,j=⟨bi,bj∗⟩⟨bj∗,bj∗⟩.b_{i}^{\ast}=b_{i}-\sum_{j<i}\mu_{i,j}b_{j}^{\ast},\qquad\mu_{i,j}=\frac{\langle b_{i},b_{j}^{\ast}\rangle}{\langle b_{j}^{\ast},b_{j}^{\ast}\rangle}.
    3. (c)

      Set k←2k\leftarrow 2.

    4. (d)

      While k≤nk\leq n, perform:

      1. i.

        Size reduction: for j=k−1,k−2,…,1j=k-1,k-2,\dots,1, set

        m:=round⁡(μk,j),bk←bk−m​bj,m:=\mathrm{round}(\mu_{k,j}),\qquad b_{k}\leftarrow b_{k}-m\,b_{j},

        and update the Gram–Schmidt data (bk∗b_{k}^{\ast}, μk,⋅\mu_{k,\cdot}).

      2. ii.

        Lovász condition check: if

        δ​‖bk−1∗‖22≤‖bk∗‖22+μk,k−12​‖bk−1∗‖22,\delta\,\|b_{k-1}^{\ast}\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|b_{k}^{\ast}\|_{2}^{2}+\mu_{k,k-1}^{2}\,\|b_{k-1}^{\ast}\|_{2}^{2},

        then set k←k+1k\leftarrow k+1 (the basis vectors bk−1,bkb_{k-1},b_{k} are well-ordered). Otherwise (swap step):

        • •

          Swap the basis vectors: (bk−1,bk)←(bk,bk−1)(b_{k-1},b_{k})\leftarrow(b_{k},b_{k-1}).

        • •

          Recompute Gram–Schmidt data for indices k−1k-1 and kk.

        • •

          Set k←max⁡{k−1,2}k\leftarrow\max\{k-1,2\}.

    5. (e)

      When the loop terminates, the vectors b1,…,bnb_{1},\dots,b_{n} form an LLL-reduced basis. Collect them into the reduced matrix B~∈ℝ(d+n)×n\tilde{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+n)\times n}.

    6. (f)

      Keep track of the unimodular transformation T∈ℤn×nT\in\mathbb{Z}^{n\times n} such that B~=Be​T\tilde{B}=B_{e}T, i.e., each reduced basis vector is an integer combination of the original ones.

  3. 3.

    Run Babai’s nearest-plane algorithm (Babai, 1986) on the reduced basis B~\tilde{B}.

    1. (a)

      Compute a QR (or Gram–Schmidt) factorization of the reduced basis:

      B~=Q​R,\tilde{B}=QR,

      where Q∈ℝ(d+n)×nQ\in\mathbb{R}^{(d+n)\times n} has orthonormal columns and R∈ℝn×nR\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is upper triangular.

    2. (b)

      Compute the coordinates of the target in the orthonormal basis:

      y:=Q⊤​t∈ℝn.y:=Q^{\top}t\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.
    3. (c)

      Initialize an integer coefficient vector z∈ℤnz\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} (e.g., z=0z=0).

    4. (d)

      For i=n,n−1,…,1i=n,n-1,\dots,1 (backwards):

      1. i.

        Compute the one-step residual

        ri:=yi−∑j=i+1nRi​j​zj.r_{i}:=y_{i}-\sum_{j=i+1}^{n}R_{ij}\,z_{j}.

        zi:=round⁡(riRi​i),z_{i}:=\mathrm{round}\!\left(\frac{r_{i}}{R_{ii}}\right),

      Map back to the original basis:

      xint:=T​z∈ℤn.x_{\mathrm{int}}:=Tz\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}.

      By construction, B~​z=Be​xint\tilde{B}z=B_{e}x_{\mathrm{int}}, so the corresponding lattice vector is

      y⁡(xint)=Be​xint−t=(V​xint+g†M​xint).y(x_{\mathrm{int}})=B_{e}x_{\mathrm{int}}-t=\begin{pmatrix}Vx_{\mathrm{int}}+g^{\dagger}\\[2.0pt] Mx_{\mathrm{int}}\end{pmatrix}.

    Truncation.

    1. (a)

      For MM large enough, the integer vector xintx_{\mathrm{int}} produced by the nearest-plane step satisfies xint∈{0,1}nx_{\mathrm{int}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}. In that case, we directly take

      x^:=xint∈{0,1}n\hat{x}:=x_{\mathrm{int}}\in\{0,1\}^{n}

    2. (b)

      If in practice some entries of xintx_{\mathrm{int}} fall outside {0,1}\{0,1\}, one may optionally project them back to {0,1}\{0,1\}, e.g.,

      x^i:=min{1,max{0,xint,i}},i=1,…,n.\hat{x}_{i}:=\min\{1,\max\{0,x_{\mathrm{int},i}\}\},\quad i=1,\dots,n.

Appendix E BAL-A: Counterexamples for Surrogate Objective Mismatch

Proposition E.1 (No universal MM yields minimum-flip recovery).

Fix any M>0M>0. There exist an instance (V,g†)(V,g^{\dagger}) for which the exact flip attack is feasible with optimal flip count K⋆=1K^{\star}=1, i.e., ∃x⋆∈{0,1}n\exists\,x^{\star}\in\{0,1\}^{n} with ‖x⋆‖0=1\|x^{\star}\|_{0}=1 and V​x⋆=−g†Vx^{\star}=-g^{\dagger}. But the minimizer of the surrogate problem minx∈{0,1}n⁡FM​(x)\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}F_{M}(x) is infeasible and hence not the optimal attack pattern. Consequently, there is no universal choice of MM that guarantees FMF_{M} recovers a feasible minimum-flip attack pattern for all instances.

Proposition E.2 (MM can enforce under-selection for any sparsity level).

Fix any integer K0≥2K_{0}\geq 2 and any residual scale r>0r>0. There exists an instance (V,g†)(V,g^{\dagger}) with optimal flip count K⋆=K0K^{\star}=K_{0}, i.e., ∃x⋆∈{0,1}n\exists\,x^{\star}\in\{0,1\}^{n} with ‖x⋆‖0=K0\|x^{\star}\|_{0}=K_{0} and V​x⋆=−g†Vx^{\star}=-g^{\dagger}, such that for any MM satisfying M2>r2M^{2}>r^{2} every minimizer x^\hat{x} of minx∈{0,1}n⁡FM​(x)\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}F_{M}(x) satisfies ‖x^‖0≤K0−1\|\hat{x}\|_{0}\leq K_{0}-1. In particular, minimizing FMF_{M} does not recover the minimum-flip solution x⋆x^{\star}.

Proposition E.1 shows that for any fixed MM there exist instances where the FMF_{M} minimizer is infeasible even though a feasible exact solution exists. This rules out a universal MM that guarantees attack success via minimizing FMF_{M}. Proposition E.2 is conceptually different: it exhibits instances with any prescribed optimum sparsity K⋆=K0K^{\star}=K_{0} for which the FMF_{M} strictly prefers an attack pattern with fewer flips. Together, these results clarify that FMF_{M} mixes two goals: (i) promoting binary structure via regularization, (ii) recovering the minimum-flip attack pattern via residual minimization. These goals can conflict, so sufficient conditions tied to each need not admit a common choice of MM on a given instance.

Appendix F BAL-A: Worst-Case Performance of BAL-A

We cite the following corollary and definition on the worst-case performance of Babai’s algorithm on LLL-reduced bases (Babai, 1986; Stephens-Davidowitz, 2016):

Corollary F.1.

For any δ∈(1/4,1]\delta\in(1/4,1], Babai’s algorithm with a δ\delta-LLL basis solves γ\gamma-CVP for γ≤n(δ−1/4)−n/2\gamma\leq\sqrt{n}\,(\delta-1/4)^{-n/2}. In particular, there is an efficient algorithm that solves γ\gamma-CVP for γ=2O⁡(n)\gamma=2^{O(n)}.

Definition F.2 (γ\gamma-CVP).

For any approximation factor γ=γ⁡(n)≥1\gamma=\gamma(n)\geq 1, the γ\gamma-Closest Vector Problem (γ\gamma-CVP) is defined as follows. The input is a basis for a lattice ℒ⊆ℝn\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} and a target vector t∈ℝnt\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. The goal is to output a lattice vector x∈ℒx\in\mathcal{L} with ‖x−t‖≤γ⋅dist​(t,ℒ)\|x-t\|\leq\gamma\cdot\text{dist}(t,\mathcal{L}).

We summarize the Binary Matching Pursuit Attack (BMP-A) algorithm in Algorithm 2.

Appendix H Experiments and Results: Setup Details

This section collects implementation details omitted from the main text.

H.1 Synthetic Dictionaries

We use synthetic VV to test the theory in a controlled way. For BMP-A, the coherence guarantee is stated for a fixed dictionary; therefore we fix a single low-coherence matrix V∈ℝ200×200V\in\mathbb{R}^{200\times 200} and sweep the sparsity level K⋆K^{\star}. We build VV by repeatedly resampling random Gaussian columns (normalized to unit norm) to reduce the maximum pairwise normalized correlation. The final constructed VV has empirical mutual coherence μ⁡(V)≈0.1971\mu(V)\approx 0.1971 and the maximum K⋆K^{\star} satisfying the condition (15) is Kcoh=3K_{\text{coh}}=3. We then run 200200 Monte Carlo trials per KK with K∈{1,…,60}K\in\{1,\dots,60\}. In each trial we sample a random support SS of size K⋆K^{\star} as the ground-truth flips x⋆x^{\star}, set −g†=∑i∈Svi-g^{\dagger}=\sum_{i\in S}v_{i}, and run BMP-A for exactly K⋆K^{\star} iterations to isolate whether the greedy rule selects the correct support as K⋆K^{\star} increases.

For BAL-A, we study the dependence on the lattice penalty MM and compare to separation thresholds. Computing the separation threshold requires combinatorial search, so we keep nn small. We use a random Gaussian dictionary with unit-norm columns, with V∈ℝ64×20V\in\mathbb{R}^{64\times 20}, K⋆=5K^{\star}=5, and 200200 Monte Carlo trials. The sufficient binary coefficient bound from (12) gives M0≈1.68817M_{0}\approx 1.68817 with B=1B=1 and R=0R=0. The Mall sepM_{\text{all sep}} that satisfies all separation conditions in (13) is computed exactly as Mall sep≈0.68287M_{\text{all sep}}\approx 0.68287. For each trial we sweep MM over 2525 log-spaced values in [0.05, 3.0][0.05,\,3.0]; we apply LLL reduction δ=0.75\delta=0.75 before Babai to improve numerical stability. With n=20n=20, we can enumerate all kk-flip candidates for k<K⋆k<K^{\star} and compute the separation threshold exactly, which is why we use this small-nn synthetic setting.

H.2 Stanford Human Preferences Dataset

We also evaluate on a real preference dataset, Stanford Human Preferences (SHP) (Ethayarajh et al., 2022), by constructing VV from a log-linear DPO pipeline. We load 20,00020{,}000 training pairs, of which each (history, response) pair is embedded with a frozen DistilBERT encoder (distilbert-base-uncased), using maximum sequence length 256256 and the [CLS] embedding. For each preference pair we form the feature difference ψi=ϕ⁡(preferred)−ϕ⁡(non-preferred)\psi_{i}=\phi(\text{preferred})-\phi(\text{non-preferred}). We train a log-linear DPO policy for 33 epochs with learning rate 10−310^{-3}, batch size 256256, and β=1\beta=1. After training, we build the attack matrix VV such that each column viv_{i} is the per-example gradient change caused by flipping the ii-th preference label.

BAL-A is expensive in the order of nn, so on SHP we randomly pick the subset of n=50n=50 for training pairs attack K⋆=7K^{\star}=7 among the subset, and run a penalty sweep over MM over 55 trials. The sufficient binary coefficient bound from (12) gives M0≈6.71994M_{0}\approx 6.71994 with B≈3.47103B\approx 3.47103 and R=0R=0. The Mall sepM_{\text{all sep}} that satisfies all separation conditions in (13) is computed exactly as Mall sep≈1.32166M_{\text{all sep}}\approx 1.32166. We use 2525 log-spaced MM values in [0.05, 10.0][0.05,\,10.0], BAL-A with LLL pre-reduction (δ=0.75\delta=0.75) to attack. Once we obtain the attack output x^\hat{x}, we evaluate support recovery against x⋆x^{\star}.

For BMP-A, we compare two subsets of the same size to isolate the effect of coherence: (i) a random subset of training pairs, and (ii) a low-coherence subset selected greedily by adding a column only if its maximum normalized inner product with the already-selected set is below a relaxed threshold. We use K⋆=10K^{\star}=10 and a relaxed threshold larger than that in (15) so that the low-coherence subset is large enough to run many trials. Note that this threshold is not required to satisfy our sufficient condition; it is used only to reduce coherence in practice. On each subset we run 200200 Monte Carlo trials: we sample K⋆K^{\star} true flips uniformly within the subset, set t=V​x⋆t=Vx^{\star}, run BMP-A with a budget up to K=K⋆+5=15K=K^{\star}+5=15, and use stopping tolerance ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3}. We report support recovery and residual curves as a function of the budget, and we also report the empirical mutual coherence of each subset to quantify how the subset construction changes VV.

We evaluate the ℓ2\ell_{2} distance of the policy parameter θ^\hat{\theta} learned by DPO on the BAL-A or BMP-A attacked subset of SHP 𝒟~​(x^)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(\hat{x}) to the parameter θ†\theta^{\dagger} learned on the ground-truth attacked subset of SHP 𝒟~​(x⋆)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x^{\star}). We also evaluate the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance of corresponding learned policies πθ^\pi_{\hat{\theta}} and πθ†\pi_{\theta^{\dagger}}, to quantify the success of the attack.

Appendix I Experiments and Results: Additional Results on SHP

This section reports the SHP experiments referenced in the main text.

I.1 BAL-A Performance on SHP

Figure 3 reports TPR of BAL-A on an SHP-derived dictionary (d=768d=768, n=50n=50, K⋆=7K^{\star}=7) as the penalty MM varies. Recovery is near-perfect for small MM, and then degrades rapidly when MM exceeds the separation threshold Msep,allM_{\text{sep,all}}, consistent with the theory. The explicit sufficient bound M0≈6.72M_{0}\approx 6.72 is conservative in this setting.

Figure 4 compares the learned model from the BAL-A attacked subset of SHP 𝒟~​(x^)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(\hat{x}) to the model learned from the ground-truth attacked subset of SHP 𝒟~​(x⋆)\tilde{\mathcal{D}}(x^{\star}), using ‖θ^−θ†‖2\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\dagger}\|_{2} in parameter space and ‖πθ^−πθ†‖1\|\pi_{\hat{\theta}}-\pi_{\theta^{\dagger}}\|_{1} in policy space. Across the full sweep of MM, both distances change only mildly, even though support recovery in Fig. 3 collapses for large MM. This weak dependence is expected in our SHP setting because the learned log-linear DPO model is trained on a limited subset (n=50n=50), so different flip sets can still yield similar fitted parameters/policies. We report these curves to check downstream policy impact, while using TPR as the primary indicator of attack success.

I.2 BMP-A Performance on SHP

Figure 5 shows that the subset construction meaningfully changes the geometry of the SHP-derived dictionary. The random subset has a much heavier right tail of pairwise normalized correlations and a larger mutual coherence (here μ≈0.807\mu\approx 0.807), while the low-coherence subset shifts the distribution left (here μ≈0.263\mu\approx 0.263).

Figure 6 compares BMP-A on two SHP-derived dictionaries with the same size (n=401n=401) but different coherence: a random subset (μ=0.807\mu=0.807, Kcoh=1K_{\mathrm{coh}}=1) and a low-coherence subset (μ=0.263\mu=0.263, Kcoh=2K_{\mathrm{coh}}=2). We sample K⋆=10K^{\star}=10 true flips and set y=V​x⋆y=Vx^{\star}, then run BMP-A with tolerance ε=10−3\varepsilon=10^{-3} up to budget tmax=15t_{\max}=15 with 200 trials. The low-coherence subset yields consistently higher TPR as the budget increases and drives the residual down faster, often reaching a near-zero residual around K⋆K^{\star}. In contrast, on the random subset BMP-A makes more incorrect selections as the budget grows, which limits support recovery and can increase the residual after additional wrong updates. Overall, reducing coherence and increasing budget improves the greedy dynamics in practice.

Figure 7 evaluates ‖θ^−θ†‖2\|\hat{\theta}-\theta^{\dagger}\|_{2} and ‖πθ^−πθ†‖1\|\pi_{\hat{\theta}}-\pi_{\theta^{\dagger}}\|_{1} for the BMP-A. Over the sweep on budget KK, both quantities change only modestly, even when the recovered support is imperfect. This is reasonable because the DPO model is trained on a larger but still limited subset (n=401n=401), so different flip sets can lead to similar fitted parameters and policies. We include these curves as a sanity check on downstream impact, while using TPR and residual reduction as the primary indicator of attack success.

J.1 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Proof.

For the log-linear policy class, we have

logπθ(a∣s)=ψ(s,a)⊤θ−log∑bexp(ψ(s,b)⊤θ),\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid s)=\psi(s,a)^{\top}\theta-\log\sum_{b}\exp(\psi(s,b)^{\top}\theta),

and similarly for μ=πθμ\mu=\pi_{\theta_{\mu}}. Therefore,

where Δ​ψi:=ψ⁡(si,ai)−ψ⁡(si,ai′)∈ℝd\Delta\psi_{i}:=\psi(s_{i},a_{i})-\psi(s_{i},a_{i}^{\prime})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Plugging into (1) gives per-sample loss

ℓi​(θ)=−log⁡σ⁡(oi​β​Δ​ψi⊤​(θ−θμ))=log⁡(1+exp⁡(−oi​β​Δ​ψi⊤​(θ−θμ))),\ell_{i}(\theta)=-\log\sigma\!\left(o_{i}\beta\Delta\psi_{i}^{\top}(\theta-\theta_{\mu})\right)=\log\!\left(1+\exp\!\left(-o_{i}\beta\Delta\psi_{i}^{\top}(\theta-\theta_{\mu})\right)\right),

since −log⁡σ⁡(t)=−log⁡(11+e−t)=log⁡(1+e−t)-\log\sigma(t)=-\log\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}\right)=\log(1+e^{-t}). Differentiating yields the per-sample gradient

gi​(θ)\displaystyle g_{i}(\theta) =∇θℓi​(θ)=−oi​β​σ​(−oi​β​Δ​ψi⊤​(θ−θμ))​Δ​ψi.\displaystyle=\nabla_{\theta}\ell_{i}(\theta)=-o_{i}\beta\,\sigma\!\left(-o_{i}\beta\Delta\psi_{i}^{\top}(\theta-\theta_{\mu})\right)\Delta\psi_{i}.

g~i​(θ)=−o~i​β​σ​(−o~i​β​Δ​ψi⊤​(θ−θμ))​Δ​ψi=oi​β​σ​(oi​β​Δ​ψi⊤​(θ−θμ))​Δ​ψi.\tilde{g}_{i}(\theta)=-\tilde{o}_{i}\beta\,\sigma\!\left(-\tilde{o}_{i}\beta\Delta\psi_{i}^{\top}(\theta-\theta_{\mu})\right)\Delta\psi_{i}=o_{i}\beta\,\sigma\!\left(o_{i}\beta\Delta\psi_{i}^{\top}(\theta-\theta_{\mu})\right)\Delta\psi_{i}.

Hence, the gradient shift is

Δ​gi​(θ)=g~i​(θ)−gi​(θ)=oi​β​σ​(oi​β​Δ​ψi⊤​(θ−θμ))​Δ​ψi+oi​β​σ​(−oi​β​Δ​ψi⊤​(θ−θμ))​Δ​ψi.\Delta g_{i}(\theta)=\tilde{g}_{i}(\theta)-g_{i}(\theta)=o_{i}\beta\,\sigma\!\left(o_{i}\beta\,\Delta\psi_{i}^{\top}(\theta-\theta_{\mu})\right)\Delta\psi_{i}+o_{i}\beta\,\sigma\!\left(-o_{i}\beta\,\Delta\psi_{i}^{\top}(\theta-\theta_{\mu})\right)\Delta\psi_{i}.
